title: Shares of spending, staffing and pay against ten like districts
question: Does San Francisco put a smaller share into classrooms, carry more administrators, or pay more per employee than like districts?
finding: In fiscal 2024 instruction took 56.9% of San Francisco's day-to-day spending against 59.1% at the middle peer (rank 9 of 11, 1 = highest share), and general plus school administration 7.0% against 6.8% (rank 4). It had 20.6 pupils per teacher against 20.8 and 222 pupils per administrator against 260. Salaries and benefits came to $150,100 per full-time-equivalent employee against $154,970 (rank 8).
how: Shares come from the federal school-finance survey; they do not depend on pupil counts, so the earlier figure shown is fiscal 2015. Staff are full-time-equivalents as the State reported them to the federal Common Core of Data for school year 2023-24 (and 2024-25 where shown), for each district's own unit; San Francisco is the district and county office together, because the county office's row carries about 1,700 of the district's support staff. Pay per employee is total salaries plus total benefits divided by total staff. Rank 1 is the highest value of the eleven.
limits: The State's staff reports to the federal file are erratic (San Francisco's teacher count is 2,827, then 3,933, then 3,189 in three successive years, as published), so staffing ratios are indications only, and a district that contracts out work such as transport or cleaning shows fewer staff and a higher figure per employee. Benefits include retiree health and pension costs set by past agreements and State law. A district where living costs are high must pay more to hire and keep staff, and one with many small schools, or with many pupils who are learning English, have disabilities or are poor, will spend more per pupil for honest reasons; none of those is measured here.
